newsitem.title: UK: European insurers gingerly study Holocaust claim.
newsitem.headline: European insurers gingerly study Holocaust claim.

text.p: European insurers are combing through old records to tot up the likely impact of a U.S. lawsuit alleging they cheated Holocaust victims out of billions of dollars during the Nazi era.
But they say they have no idea yet whether they will have to pay out and if so, how much it will cost them.

"We take this complex issue extremely seriously and will be busy looking at it but in terms of the actual content, it is very difficult to say anything yet," said a spokesman for Germany's largest insurer, Allianz .
Allianz, fellow German insurer Bavarian Reinsurance, Italian companies Generali and RAS and French firm AGF are among seven firms mentioned in the U.S. lawsuit filed on Monday.
The issue first came to light several weeks ago when Generali faced questioning over policies sold in pre-war eastern Europe.
Allianz and RAS, now a subsidiary of Allianz, have confirmed that they have made payments in similar, individual cases in the past.

Austrian insurer Wiener Allianz, also part of Allianz, said it would reimburse genuine claims. Another Austrian firm named in the lawsuit, Der Anker Allgemeine Versicherung AG, a unit of Swiss Helvetia , has remained silent.

The lawsuit alleges that Allianz and other defendants encouraged European citizens who feared persecution by the Nazis to deposit their assets with them and to purchase insurance to safeguard their family's futures.

In the class action suit on behalf of more than 10,000 people, the Holocaust victims and their families allege that the insurers withheld, concealed or converted the cash value and proceeds of policies sold before 1946 worth billions of dollars.
Allianz said there are currently no open cases and it could not say how much had been paid out so far.
Generali said last month that reports that it could be liable for tens of thousands of life insurance claims from descendants of Holocaust victims were without foundation.

Like other insurers, Generali cited problems with tracing records which were lost or destroyed in the war and its immediate aftermath, when Europe was divided into East and West by the so-called Iron Curtain.
It was Generali's takeover last month of Migdal, an Israeli insurer, that focused attention on the issue of compensation from insurers for Holocaust victims.

Lloyd's of London has never been heavily involved in life assurance and a spokesman for the market said it was unlikely any of the Holocaust related policies would have found their way back to the London-based market.
Austrian Jewish leaders called on the insurance companies to respond more quickly than Swiss banks did when they were accused of not returning Nazi gold taken from Jews.

"In the Swiss banks we have an excellent example of how not to behave in the first few weeks, and a good example of how to behave subsequently in the setting up of a holocaust fund," said cultural community president Paul Grosz.
